title: New Blood Test Maps Amino Acid Networks to Predict Colorectal Cancer Return
excerpt: South Korean researchers have developed a machine-learning framework that analyzes interactions among circulating amino acids, outperforming conventional cancer markers in predicting recurrence and metastasis.
body:
• A joint KAIST-hospital team developed a blood test that maps how 18 circulating amino acids interact, revealing metabolic changes tied to cancer progression.
  • The combined model outperformed CEA-only testing — the current clinical standard — in predicting recurrence and metastasis after colorectal cancer surgery.
  • Separately, a Moffitt Cancer Center study found that DNA-based blood markers called protein EpiScores improved recurrence prediction accuracy from 64% to 70%.
  • Colorectal cancer is the third most common cancer worldwide; these advances could help personalize post-surgical monitoring using a simple blood draw.

A single blood draw taken before surgery may soon offer clinicians a sharper picture of whether colorectal cancer will return — and how aggressively.

Researchers at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), working with Gangnam Severance Hospital and Asan Medical Center, have built a machine-learning framework that maps the interaction network among 18 circulating amino acids in the blood. The approach, published in Advanced Science on June 9, 2026, outperformed the conventional carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) blood test widely used in post-operative cancer surveillance.

Beyond Individual Markers

Traditional blood-based cancer monitoring measures the concentrations of individual biomarkers in isolation. The KAIST team took a different approach: instead of tracking each amino acid separately, they analyzed how pairs of amino acids correlate and shift together as the disease progresses.

Using fluorine-19 nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy to quantify amino acids from a small serum sample, the researchers found that the amino acid network undergoes "stage-dependent remodeling." As colorectal cancer advances, branched-chain amino acids such as valine and leucine — essential for muscle and energy metabolism — decline in relative abundance. Meanwhile, glycine and serine, which cancer cells consume to synthesize DNA and proliferate, rise.

"We hope this will lead to new precision medicine technologies that can predict recurrence risk more accurately using a blood sample alone and help establish personalized treatment strategies."

— Professor Ji Min Lee, KAIST

The study is the first to demonstrate that the interaction network among circulating amino acids can function as a blood-based metabolic biomarker for colorectal cancer progression.

A Growing Arsenal of Blood-Based Tests

The KAIST study adds to a growing body of research seeking to replace or supplement invasive follow-up procedures. In February 2026, Moffitt Cancer Center published findings in Clinical Epigenetics identifying four protein EpiScores — markers based on chemical modifications to blood cell DNA — that were strongly associated with worse outcomes. Patients with elevated levels faced a 60% to 70% higher risk of recurrence. When combined with standard clinical factors such as cancer stage and age, these markers improved recurrence prediction accuracy from 64% to 70%.

Separately, the Phase II GALAXY study, presented at the ESMO Gastrointestinal Cancers Congress in July 2026, found that circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) detected after surgery identified patients with more than four times the recurrence risk. Among ctDNA-positive patients who received chemotherapy, the risk of recurrence dropped by 93% compared with those who did not.

Why It Matters for Clinical Practice

Colorectal cancer is the third most common cancer globally and the second-leading cause of cancer death. Current post-operative monitoring relies heavily on CEA blood tests and periodic imaging, but a 2017 analysis of the UK's FACS trial found that a single CEA test at the standard threshold missed more than half of recurrences. The limitations of existing tools have driven research into more sensitive, blood-based alternatives.

The new approaches differ in their targets — amino acid metabolism, epigenetic patterns, and tumor DNA fragments — but share a common ambition: extracting more predictive information from a routine blood draw. None is ready for clinical adoption yet; all require validation in larger, more diverse patient populations. But as Professor Per Pfeiffer of Odense University Hospital noted regarding the ctDNA findings, the results suggest that blood tests "could help doctors identify which patients are most likely to benefit from chemotherapy after surgery, while potentially sparing others unnecessary treatment."

What to Watch

The KAIST team plans to develop the amino acid network analysis into a clinical-grade diagnostic tool. The Moffitt group is pursuing validation studies in additional patient cohorts. And the ctDNA field continues to grow, with tissue-free assays like Guardant Reveal already demonstrating clinical utility in detecting minimal residual disease with 98.2% specificity.

For patients and clinicians navigating the uncertainty of post-operative surveillance, the message is cautiously optimistic: the era of one-size-fits-all monitoring may be drawing to a close.
